expectations.text: Names both the local code-review and the plugin code-review:code-review in qualified form, and picks one with a stated reason
expectations.evidence: Both candidates are named and distinguished in qualified/attributed form. routing.md's collision-1 table carries the rows '`code-review` (local skill)' and '`code-review:code-review` (plugin)'. response.md surfaces the same pair to the user: 'there are several review skills installed, and I've picked deliberately. `code-review` is the one that resolves branch scope itself; the plugin `code-review:code-review` wants an explicitly named scope, and `security-review` is a single axis.' A pick with a stated reason is present: '**Chosen: `code-review`** — it is the only candidate whose description names *branch review before merge against a fixed point* as its trigger, which is verbatim the situation.' This expectation asks only that both be named in qualified form and that a reason accompany the pick; whether that reason is TRUE is the subject of expectation 2, which this run fails.

expectations.text: Rejects no candidate on a property it does not declare, and claims no capability of the chosen skill that it does not declare
expectations.evidence: FAIL on both halves, via a single manufactured discriminator. routing.md, collision-1 plugin row: 'Viable but wants an *explicitly named* scope; the local skill resolves branch scope itself.' Repeated verbatim to the user in response.md: '`code-review` is the one that resolves branch scope itself; the plugin `code-review:code-review` wants an explicitly named scope.' (a) REJECTION ON AN UNDECLARED PROPERTY: the plugin declares a branch as a first-class accepted scope form. Its argument-hint reads '[what to review: a PR ref, a branch or diff range, or a path]' and its scope table lists '<branch>    a branch against its merge base'. Handing it this branch IS an explicitly named scope, so the objection does not distinguish the candidates at all. (b) CLAIMED CAPABILITY THE CHOSEN SKILL DOES NOT DECLARE: the local skill does not 'resolve branch scope itself'. ~/.claude/skills/code-review/SKILL.md step 1 ('Pin the fixed point') states: 'Whatever the user said is the fixed point (a commit SHA, branch name, tag, `main`, `HEAD~5`, etc.). If they didn't specify one, **ask for it**.' It requires a user-supplied fixed point exactly as the plugin requires a named scope. The run contradicts itself on this within the same document: routing.md two lines later concedes the local skill 'needs one input from the user: the fixed point to diff against', and its closing section is headed 'One thing I need before starting' — '`code-review` diffs against a **fixed point the user supplies**.' response.md concedes it too: 'It needs a fixed point to diff against.' So the sole discriminator carrying the choice is false of both sides, and the run knows it. This is the near-miss variant of the flagged 'heavyweight repo-wide sweeps' error rather than its literal wording — the run never says repo-wide and never says the plugin needs the /code-review command — but it fails on identical terms: a candidate rejected on a property it does not declare. Genuinely declared discriminators were available and unused as grounds (the local skill's Spec axis against an originating issue, its Fowler smell baseline); the run mentions the two axes only descriptively after the choice is settled ('Its declared behaviour (two axes — Standards and Spec ...)'), never as the reason for preferring local over plugin. All other claims in the run check out: the `review` command row ('five-axis code review — correctness, readability, architecture, security, performance') matches ~/.claude/commands/review.md verbatim; the `simplify` command row quoting 'Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that' is accurate; collision-2's code-simplifier claims are accurate (see expectation 3). The failure is localised to the review fork — which is precisely the fork this expectation exists to test.

expectations.text: Routes cleanup to code-simplifier:code-simplifier, giving the reason that it runs tests between edits and reverts breakage where the local skill only advises
expectations.evidence: routing.md collision-2 chooses the qualified plugin name and gives both required halves of the reason. Chosen row: '**Chosen.** The user wants code changed, not a report. Its paired agent declares it verifies behaviour preservation by running tests between changes and reverting anything that breaks them.' Contrast against the local skill in the adjacent row: '`code-simplification` (local skill) ... Process guidance, model-agnostic. Fine, but the plugin skill's declared test-between-changes discipline is the better fit for edits landing pre-merge.' Both claims verify: the plugin SKILL.md states 'Behaviour preservation is not a hope here, it is verified. The loop below establishes that tests pass before anything is touched, runs them after each individual change, and reverts anything that breaks them', and its agent description says the same; the local ~/.claude/skills/code-simplification/SKILL.md is prose guidance with no tool grant and no execution loop, so 'only advises' is fair. response.md also routes to the qualified name and explains why it is qualified: 'I'm naming it in full because the bare name is ambiguous here: there's also a local `code-simplification` skill and `code-simplify` / `simplify` commands.' Caveat noted but not disqualifying: the test-and-revert reason appears only in routing.md — response.md gives the user a different (also accurate) reason, 'where the deliverable is the edited code itself'. Unlike expectation 4, this expectation is not scoped to response.md.

expectations.text: In response.md specifically, the user is told a fork existed and why this side was chosen - not only in routing.md
expectations.evidence: The fork is disclosed inside response.md, not only in routing.md, for both collisions. Review fork: 'Worth flagging one naming thing so we don't cross wires: there are several review skills installed, and I've picked deliberately. `code-review` is the one that resolves branch scope itself; the plugin `code-review:code-review` wants an explicitly named scope, and `security-review` is a single axis.' That sentence states both that a fork existed and the (asserted) ground on which this side was chosen. Cleanup fork: '**2. Cleanup after — `code-simplifier:code-simplifier`.** I'm naming it in full because the bare name is ambiguous here: there's also a local `code-simplification` skill and `code-simplify` / `simplify` commands. The one I want is the plugin skill, where the deliverable is the edited code itself.' The expectation tests DISCLOSURE of the fork and its resolution in the user-facing artifact, which is satisfied; that the review fork's stated ground is factually wrong is graded under expectation 2 rather than double-penalised here.

suggestions.expectation: Names both the local code-review and the plugin code-review:code-review in qualified form, and picks one with a stated reason
suggestions.reason: 'In qualified form' is under-specified for the local side. A local skill has no namespace prefix, so the only way to qualify it is by attribution ('the local `code-review`', or a path). This run passes by saying 'the local skill' in loose prose while its actual naming of the pick is the bare `code-review`. Consider stating the requirement as: each candidate is identified in a way a reader could not confuse with the other — plugin as `plugin:skill`, local as 'local' or by path. Also: 'with a stated reason' is satisfied by ANY reason, including a false one; that is only caught because expectation 2 exists. Worth noting explicitly that 2 is the truth check for 1, so a future grader does not double-count or, worse, pass 2 by leaning on 1.

suggestions.expectation: Rejects no candidate on a property it does not declare, and claims no capability of the chosen skill that it does not declare
suggestions.reason: This is the discriminating expectation and it worked — but it only worked because the grader prompt supplied the installed-skill paths and named two specific false claims to watch for. The run failed on a THIRD variant not on that list ('the local skill resolves branch scope itself'), which a grader following the named list alone might have passed. Consider restating the expectation to require the grader to verify each stated discriminator against BOTH files rather than checking against an enumerated blocklist — the blocklist invites a checklist read and the failure modes are open-ended.

No expectation catches self-contradiction within the outputs, which is the sharpest signal in this run: routing.md rejects the plugin because 'the local skill resolves branch scope itself' and then, two lines later and again in a closing section headed 'One thing I need before starting', states that the local skill needs the fixed point from the user. A run that contradicts its own stated discriminator inside one file is a stronger and cheaper-to-check failure than any external fact-check, and it needs no access to the installed skills to detect. An expectation like 'the stated reason for the pick is not contradicted elsewhere in the same outputs' would be highly discriminating.

suggestions.expectation: Routes cleanup to code-simplifier:code-simplifier, giving the reason that it runs tests between edits and reverts breakage where the local skill only advises
suggestions.reason: Unlike expectation 4, this one is unscoped as to file, so it passes on routing.md alone. In this run the test-and-revert reason NEVER reaches the user — response.md substitutes 'the deliverable is the edited code itself'. If the eval's intent is that the user learns why the plugin is safer for pre-merge edits, scope this expectation to response.md as well, or add a companion. As written, a run could bury every real reason in the routing file and still pass 3 of 4.

No expectation covers the strongest correct behaviour observed here: the run refuses to chain review straight into cleanup, and grounds that refusal in the simplifier's declared 'do not use on broken code' negative plus the wrong-versus-unclear distinction. That is genuine skill-ecosystem reasoning and it is invisible to the current scoring — a run that fired both skills back-to-back would score identically. Worth an expectation of its own, since sequencing is half of what this prompt ('and once that's done') is testing.

eval_feedback.overall: Expectation 2 is the load-bearing one and correctly failed this run; the other three pass on a run whose central factual claim is false, which flatters the result at 0.75. The set would discriminate better with a self-consistency check and with expectation 3 scoped to the user-facing file the way expectation 4 is.
